# The case study record

Case Study Core, `schema_version: 1`. Status: draft for the owner's approval.

One record, produced by both tracks. Track 1 is the WordPress plugin working on its own. Track 2 is YourTradeQuotes (YTQ). Every output (a page, its JSON-LD, a social post, a feed entry) is made from this record and from nothing else.

The schema is `core/schema/case-study.v1.schema.json` (JSON Schema 2020-12). This document explains it. Where the two disagree, the schema and the fixtures win and this file is wrong.

## 1. Order of steps when a case study is written

The same on both routes:

1. **Details.** Service, town, month, and the facts of the job in the author's own words.
2. **AI draft.** Straight after the details. Optional in Track 1, where the client can write every answer by hand.
3. **Edit.** A person reads and changes the draft.
4. **Photos.** Chosen, given a role, given alt text, and ticked one by one (section 4).
5. **Permission.** The consent record (`consent.md`). Always the last step before publish.
6. **Publish.** The software that publishes runs the validator and refuses if it fails.

Permission is last on purpose: the person confirming it has just seen the exact words and photos that will go out.

## 2. Fields

| Field | Rule |
|---|---|
| `schema_version` | `1` |
| `id` | 8 to 64 characters from `A-Z a-z 0-9 _ -`, starting with a letter or digit. Stable for the life of the case study. **Generated by the software** (Track 1 a UUID, Track 2 its document id), never built from a name, a place or a job number. It is scanned like text (`privacy.md`), and **checked when it is made**: see below |
| `version` | Integer from 1. See section 5 |
| `source` | `wordpress` or `ytq`: where it was written |
| `status` | `draft`, `published` or `unpublished` |
| `title` | 10 to 110 characters. Suggested as service, town, month and year, then made unique on the site. Editable |
| `slug` | Lower-case letters, digits and single hyphens, 3 to 96 characters |
| `excerpt` | 20 to 200 characters. Used as the meta description and on listing cards |
| `service_category` | 2 to 60 characters. One term from the site's or account's own list |
| `location.town` | Town only. Letters, spaces, full stops, apostrophes and hyphens, so a postcode or house number cannot be stored |
| `location.show_town` | `false` hides the town everywhere: page, JSON-LD, social text. The validator then refuses any public text that names it |
| `completed_month` | `YYYY-MM`. A day cannot be stored |
| `sections` | **Three to five** of the five question-led sections, each `{key, question, answer}`, in the fixed order `need`, `challenge`, `solution`, `work`, `result`, no key twice. **`work` (what was done) is always present.** A section the facts cannot answer is left out, never padded. The question (8 to 140 characters) is the heading. The answer is 20 to 1,500 characters |
| `faqs` | 0 to 4 `{question, answer}`. Each must be answerable from the job's own facts. None is better than an invented one |
| `photos` | 1 to 12. Section 4 |
| `consent` | `consent.md`. Required once status is `published` or `unpublished` |
| `social` | Optional `{caption, link_label}`. `social.md` |
| `published_at` | When version 1 first went live. UTC, `YYYY-MM-DDTHH:MM:SSZ`. Never changes afterwards |
| `modified_at` | When this version was published. Same format |
| `unpublished_at` | Present only while status is `unpublished` |

Text rules, for every text field:

- Plain text. No HTML and no Markdown. Renderers escape it.
- **Line breaks belong in answers only.** Inside a section or FAQ answer a line break is a paragraph break, and it may arrive as LF, CR LF (what a browser form sends) or a bare CR: all three are accepted as they are, and a renderer treats each as one paragraph break. Anywhere else, including the title, a line break is refused (`text.line_break`).
- A tab is accepted and treated as a space.
- Minimum lengths count what a reader would see: spaces and line breaks at the ends, repeated spaces and invisible characters do not count, so a title of ten spaces is too short. Maximum lengths count every character.
- No other control characters (`text.control_character`).
- No styled or enclosed letters and digits, such as mathematical bold or circled numbers (`text.unsupported_character`). The content checks cannot read them. Ordinary accented letters, symbols and emoji are fine.

Timestamps are the publication's own times. They are not job dates. The only date about the job is the month. A timestamp must be a real calendar date.

Numbers are whole numbers no larger than 9,007,199,254,740,991, the largest both languages hold exactly.

**Ids and photo refs are checked when they are made.** The content checks run on `id` and `ref`, and an id cannot be reworded, so one that happens to look like a postcode or a reference (`abcd_M1-1AE_xyz9`, `QUO_55218xyz`) would make its case study unpublishable for ever. So the software that generates an id or ref calls `isSafeIdentifier(value)` (Node) or `Privacy::isSafeIdentifier($value)` (PHP) straight away and generates another if the answer is false. For a UUID or a random 20-character id that almost never happens (none in 200,000 of each), but "almost never" is not good enough for something that cannot be fixed later.

## 3. What can never be present

Customer name, contact details, address, postcode, coordinates, job or quote reference, exact job dates, prices, internal notes, signatures.

This is enforced in two layers.

- **By construction.** Every object in the schema has `additionalProperties: false`. There is no field for any of these, so a record carrying `customer_name` or `postcode` is refused by name whatever its value. The town pattern rejects digits. The month pattern has no day. **Records are strict:** a reader rejects a record carrying a field it does not know (`versioning.md`).
- **By content.** The free text fields, and the id and photo refs, are scanned before publish (`privacy.md`).

A track must not keep a second, looser copy of the record for its own convenience. If a track needs private working data (the job id it came from, the customer's own details for the forbidden-term check), that lives beside the record in the track's own storage and is never sent anywhere.

## 4. Photos

Each photo is `{ref, role, alt, caption?, order, pair?, width, height, sha256, checked}`.

| Field | Rule |
|---|---|
| `ref` | Opaque handle generated by the software, same character set as `id`. Never a URL, a file name, or anything built from a name or an address: it ends up in public file names, and it is scanned like text |
| `role` | `hero`, `before`, `after` or `other`. **Exactly one `hero`** |
| `alt` | 5 to 160 characters, describing what is in the picture |
| `caption` | Optional, up to 200 characters |
| `order` | 1 to 12, unique within the record |
| `pair` | Optional, 1 to 6. Ties one `before` to one `after`. Each pair number is used by exactly one of each. A before or after photo without a pair is shown in the gallery with its label |
| `width`, `height` | Pixels of the published derivative, 320 to 2,560. **A hero under 1,200 pixels wide is allowed.** The validator returns the warning `photos.hero_narrow` and the authoring screen shows it; it does not stop a publish |
| `sha256` | Of the published derivative, after metadata was stripped |
| `checked` | The person's tick: `{confirmed: true, confirmed_by, confirmed_at}` |

**The tick.** Before a photo is used, a person confirms it shows no faces, number plates, house numbers or documents. The exact words are in `core/schema/consent-wording.v1.json` (`photo_check`). Rules for both tracks:

- It is never ticked by default and never ticked in bulk by one "select all" control.
- It is never written by AI. An AI response is not allowed to contain `checked`, and a track must drop the field from anything a model returns.
- `confirmed_by` and `confirmed_at` are set by the server from the signed-in person and the server clock, not taken from the request body.
- The schema has no `false` value and no bare `true`. A tick either carries who and when or it is absent. A published record with any photo missing its tick is invalid.
- A tick is never dated after the publish it belongs to (`photos.checked_after_publish`), and never after the permission that covers it (`consent.confirmed_before_photo_tick`): permission is the last step.
- The tick on a photo that has not changed is carried over exactly, or the photo is ticked again; it cannot be quietly rewritten (`transition.photo_tick_changed`).
- Replacing a photo's file (a new `sha256`) or adding a photo needs a new tick (`transition.photo_tick_not_fresh`). On an edit of a live case study, and on publishing again after an unpublish, the tick is dated after the previous version went live. On a draft, a replaced file needs a tick later than the one the old file had.

**Role suggestions (YTQ).** YTQ may suggest which photo is the hero and which are before and after. In the first release the suggestion comes **from metadata and timing only**: which set the photo was added to and when it was taken. No photo is sent to an AI service; that would be a later opt-in with its own wording. A suggestion is shown as a suggestion the person can change, and becomes the photo's role only when the person leaves or sets it and ticks the photo. The record does not store who suggested the role.

## 5. Status and version

```
draft -> published -> unpublished -> published (always needs a new consent record)
            |
            +-> edit (a separate working copy) -> published as version n+1, same id, same URL
```

- `id` plus `version` is the idempotency key for publishing and delivery: feeds, site upserts, acknowledgements, retries. Sending the same pair twice changes nothing. (Social posts are different: they are claimed once per case study and network, whatever the version. See `social.md` section 5.)
- **A published version never changes.** Two records with the same `id` and `version` are identical in every field, or one of them is wrong (`transition.same_version_changed`). Any change, however small, is the next version.
- A new case study is a draft at version 1. Its first publish is version 1.
- Each later publish is exactly one higher. Unpublish does not change the version.
- A published record never goes back to `draft`. An edit is a working copy held by the track; the live version stays live until the copy is published as the next version.
- `published_at` is fixed at the first publish. `modified_at` moves forward on every publish.
- **Unpublish changes only three things:** the status, `unpublished_at`, and the withdrawal on the consent record (`transition.content_changed`).
- **An unpublished record is frozen** (`transition.unpublished_frozen`). Nothing about it changes, including when and why it was unpublished, until it is published again as the next version.
- Publishing again after an unpublish always needs a consent record confirmed after the unpublish, and a publish time after it.
- A record whose consent has been withdrawn cannot have status `published`.

**When an edit needs fresh permission.** Only when it does one of three things:

1. adds a photo or changes a photo's file,
2. changes the location (the town, or whether it is shown),
3. changes the kind of permission (`customer_permission`).

Then the consent record must be confirmed after the previous version went live (`transition.consent_not_fresh`). Any other edit, including all text, reuses the existing consent record: it must then be carried over exactly as it was, or confirmed again (`transition.consent_changed` if it was altered without a new confirmation). Removing a photo is not adding or changing one. The same narrow rule applies to a draft before its first publication: permission already recorded on the draft survives a text edit and does not survive a new photo, a changed location or a changed kind of permission.

`checkTransition(previous, next)` in both reference implementations enforces all of this between two stored states. Given something that is not a record (a published record with no consent, say) it returns `transition.invalid_record`; it does not fail. `core/fixtures/transitions.json` holds 42 cases.

A receiving site does not run `checkTransition`. It upserts by version (`feed.md`).

## 6. Validation result

`validateRecord(record, {forbiddenTerms})` returns `{valid, errors, warnings}`. Each entry is `{code, path, message}`; `path` is a JSON Pointer into the record. Entries are sorted by path, then code, in Unicode code point order. Warnings never affect `valid`. Both implementations return the same result for the same input, and the fixtures hold them to it.

An option the validator does not know, or a forbidden term that is not exactly `{label, value}`, **throws**. A misspelt option used to mean the customer-detail check was silently skipped.

| Rule | Code | Path |
|---|---|---|
| Field that is not part of a case study | `schema.additional_property` | the field |
| Missing consent on a published record | `schema.required` | `/consent` |
| Not exactly one hero | `schema.contains` | `/photos` |
| No `work` section | `schema.contains` | `/sections` |
| Sections out of order or a key used twice | `sections.order` | `/sections/n/key` |
| Photo not ticked | `schema.required` | `/photos/n/checked` |
| "Not identifiable" without its ticked statement | `schema.required` | `/consent/not_identifiable_statement` |
| Withdrawn permission on a published record; the statement with another kind of permission | `schema.not_allowed` | the field |
| Other schema failures | `schema.type`, `schema.const`, `schema.enum`, `schema.pattern`, `schema.min_length`, `schema.max_length`, `schema.minimum`, `schema.maximum`, `schema.min_items`, `schema.max_items`, `schema.number_out_of_range` | the value |
| Photo order, ref and pair rules | `photos.order_duplicate`, `photos.ref_duplicate`, `photos.pair_role`, `photos.pair_incomplete` | the photo field |
| Times | `dates.invalid_calendar_date`, `dates.modified_before_published`, `dates.completed_after_published`, `dates.unpublished_before_modified`, `consent.withdrawn_before_confirmed`, `consent.confirmed_after_publish`, `consent.confirmed_before_photo_tick`, `photos.checked_after_publish` | the field |
| Social caption | `social.sentence_count`, `social.contains_link` | `/social/caption` |
| Text hygiene | `text.invalid_unicode`, `text.control_character`, `text.line_break`, `text.unsupported_character` | the text field |
| Forbidden content | `privacy.*` (`privacy.md`) | the text field |
| Warning: narrow hero | `photos.hero_narrow` | `/photos/n/width` |

`assertPublishable` is `validateRecord` plus "status is `published`". It is the gate to call before anything goes live. It does not look at whether the permission wording has been through legal review; `consent.md` section 4 says who enforces that.

The rules a schema cannot state (section order, photo, date and social rules) run only when the schema passes. The text hygiene and forbidden content checks always run.

Section order and uniqueness are checked by the reference validators, not by the schema file, so a general JSON Schema validator on its own accepts sections in any order. Everything else in the table's first rows is in the schema file.

## 7. Reading JSON

Both implementations refuse the same documents: text that is not valid JSON, a string holding half of a surrogate pair, a key that starts with a NUL character, and anything nested more than 63 levels deep. In PHP that is `Files::decode`; in Node it is `decode`, which wraps `JSON.parse` with those limits. A track that parses JSON some other way must pass the result through the validator, which reports `text.invalid_unicode` for a broken string.

## 8. What each track must do

- Run the validator on the server at publish, with the track's own vendored copy of the core. A browser check is a convenience, never the gate.
- Run `checkTransition` against the last stored state before storing a new one.
- Refuse to publish on any error. There is no override and no "publish anyway". Show warnings and let the person carry on.
- Supply forbidden terms where it knows them. Track 2 knows the customer's name, email, phone and street line and must pass them. Track 1 never collects them and passes none.
- Generate ids and photo refs itself, check each with `isSafeIdentifier` as it is made, and generate again on a false. Never derive them from anything a person typed.
- Keep the fixtures passing. No change to the record, a template or a post format ships without the fixture changing in the same pull request (`versioning.md`).
